newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU presidency sets 45 pct opening of EU gas market.
newsitem.headline: EU presidency sets 45 pct opening of EU gas market.

text.p: Luxembourg, which holds the European Union presidency, is circulating a proposal to open up 45 percent of the EU's natural gas market to competition over a 10-year period, a European Commission official said on Friday.
Luxembourg proposes that "opening of the market should start at 28 percent and go up to a maximum of 45 percent over a period of 10 years," the official told Reuters.

He welcomed the decision to pencil precise figures into the latest draft of a directive which, if adopted as hoped in December, will commit the EU's 15 member states to partial liberalisation of their gas markets.
Moves to open up the gas sector follow an agreement last December to liberalise the EU electricity sectors by an initial 23 percent.
An earlier gas proposal from the Netherlands, which EU energy ministers discussed -- but did not endorse -- on May 27, steered clear of numbers.
Luxembourg's latest draft proposed that in the first wave of liberalisation, consumers of over 25 million cubic metres of gas a year should be allowed to buy competitively, the official said.
The threshold for "eligible customers" would be cut in later stages to 15 and then five million cubic metres.

The cabinet of EU Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis and member state experts were studying the proposal and might be able to say in September if they thought ministers could provisionally endorse it in October, the official said.

Britain, a strong advocate of liberalisation, saw the proposal as "very much a move forward", though London would be pushing for even greater market opening, a British diplomat told Reuters, echoing comments made on Thursday by British Energy Minister John Battle.

Britain wanted the threshold for eligible customers to start at 15 million cubic metres and drop to one million over 10 years, he said, though he acknowledged a majority of EU states seemed happy with a 25 million cubic metres starting point.
The officials said Luxembourg had also tabled a new formula for tackling long-term take-or-pay contracts, which are popular with buyers and suppliers but are regarded as anti-competitive.

The Grand Duchy suggests national authorities should be allowed to exempt certain existing or future take-or-pay contracts from the competition rules of the directive but only once the Commission had approved the decision.
London welcomed this increase in Commission control over take-or-pay contracts but was unhappy with the vagueness of the criteria for deciding derogations, the British diplomat said.
It remains to be seen whether the Luxembourg proposals will satisfy the concerns of all EU states.
The Commission official said France was likely to resist moves towards significant levels of competition, though he hoped a compromise could be found, as in the case of electricity.
The British diplomat said he foresaw problems over provisions for allowing newcomers to use existing gas distribution networks.

The draft directive says a national gas undertaking may deny third parties access to its pipeline system if its public service obligations or take-or-pay contracts leave it with insufficient capacity.
The text says governments may be able to force incumbents to expand their pipeline capacity if this is economically feasible.
London did not believe there would be effective third party access unless the member states were obliged to impose new pipeline investments on incumbents, the diplomat said.
But Germany, which operates on a system of competing pipeline networks rather than on third party access to existing grids, was unlikely to agree to this, he said.
French and German energy officials were unavailable for comment. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
